articles.title: Why stability is elusive
articles.content: RECENT events are another reminder of how elusive political stability remains in the country. The confrontation between PTI and the government escalated after an effort at dialogue between them ended in mutual recriminations. PTI pressed ahead with its protest march that the federal government tried to stop by threatening to oust the KP government through imposition of governor’s rule. The usual wave of arrests of party activists preceded the opposition’s march. Now the Shehbaz Sharif government has imposed an emergency  and governor’s rule in KP in a move that is likely inflame sentiment in the province and exacerbate the situation. This is a rerun of a familiar script, except it is set against a backdrop of deepening authoritarianism. It also marks a dangerous phase in confrontational politics with the federal authorities and the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government at loggerheads. Inflammatory rhetoric by federal ministers was matched by fiery speeches from KP’s Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. Other than the brief interlude of dialogue, the government responded to the opposition protest by its usual mix of coercion, threats, and incendiary statements. It took the consequential decision to impose an emergency in KP and bring the province under federal control. The cabinet has approved this while parliament has been convened to sanction the move. The most egregious use of coercion was the reported abductions and incommunicado detention of over eight PTI MPs, including three members of the National Assembly. Using coercive means to manage the opposition has only reinforced the government’s slide into authoritarianism, which has resulted in the country’s democratic decline. This has been evidenced in the past couple of years in actions taken against the opposition and other critics: banning public gatherings, breaking up protest demonstrations, arresting opposition supporters, raiding homes of political leaders, filing cases against them, policing the media, imposing internet restrictions and criminalising free speech. Another telling indicator of democratic regression is the undermining of judicial independence by controversial amendments and defiance of court orders. The erosion of institutions meant to check executive power has contributed to growing autocratisation. The shell of democracy remains, but it is increasingly hollowed out. The aim of these actions is to tighten the government’s grip on the political system and the country. But it does not make the government strong. It signals weakness, not confidence. Some argue there is nothing new in this phase of repression, that it continues a familiar tradition and borrows from a well-worn playbook. Previous civilian governments, too, were guilty of undemocratic conduct, intolerance of opposition, jailing rivals on trumped-up charges, marginalising parliament, curbing press freedom, and undermining judicial independence. All of this is true. But the scale and scope of the repressive measures today go beyond anything seen under a civilian government before. Using coercive measures and undermining institutions do not produce stability. Public space is being encroached upon in an unprecedented manner. Because there is more to control in the digital era, especially social media, the present government has gone much further than its civilian predecessors in imposing digital space curbs and censorship and micromanaging the electronic media. The rationale offered by spokesmen of the hybrid government, when pressed to justify such measures, is that they are necessary for political stability. But does the veneer of calm imposed by force bring stability? On the contrary, it is a recipe for instability. Coercion does not produce stability. It deepens polarisation, erodes the social contract, divides the country further, and fuels uncertainty. The opposition represents a large section of society, has a significant parliamentary presence, and runs the government in KP. To suppress and demonise it does not promote stability. It guarantees the continuation of political confrontation. The economic cost of relentless political tensions and government-opposition conflict is plain to see. Frequent shutdowns and blockade of cities hit businesses hard. It vitiates the business climate. This at a time when recovery has yet to take hold, economic growth remains anaemic and stabilisation is still fragile. Jittery investors hold back, deterred by the spectre of turmoil and unrest. Celebrating every tranche received from the IMF doesn’t obscure the reality that the economy is yet to embark on the path to sustainable growth. Meanwhile, all recent surveys — Gallup, Ipsos — show declining public confidence in economic conditions and pessimism about the country’s economic future. Clearly, the country’s economic problems cannot be tackled in a politically volatile environment. Political stability requires a reset on several fronts. It needs the creation of a peaceful and predictable political environment resting on a truce and mutual accommodation between the government and opposition. A divided and polarised country cannot be stable. Genuine dialogue is needed that is aimed at a lasting modus vivendi, not driven by short-term expediency to stop the next protest march. It also means the government relenting in its inhumane treatment of PTI leader Imran Khan in defiance of court orders. The recent talks were doomed when the government wasn’t even willing to allow opposition leaders to meet Khan for consultations on the negotiations. It also remains unwilling to grant him his entitlement under the law. Such an attitude cannot form the basis for serious negotiations, let alone a political settlement. Political stability is also achieved by governing the country inclusively by consensus and not by excluding other political actors who command substantial electoral and public support. A ‘winner-takes-all’ approach has long characterised Pakistan’s politics. This has rested on the mistaken assumption that the party that wins an election (almost always on a minority vote and, in the case of the present government, in a disputed poll) is the ‘sole representative’ of the people. This stance leads to inherently unstable and exclusionary governance. Unilateral rule not only erodes democracy; it also undermines effective governance. The country’s federal nature makes inclusive governance essential. The centre must work with and not against opposition-run provinces. Political stability is also built by ensuring an environment where the rule of law prevails. It involves strengthening institutions and not weakening them in pursuit of ephemeral ‘control’. Strong institutions ensure predictability — the bedrock of stability. They provide the checks and balances that are essential to prevent the abuse of power and protect fundamental rights and civil liberties. To those who believe stability can be achieved by ousting an elected provincial government, concentrating power and discarding democratic freedoms, Pakistan’s history stands testimony to how disastrous that path has been for the country and its people. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
articles.author: Maleeha Lodhi

articles.title: A theorist of crisis
articles.content: BORN in Karachi in 1945, Anwar Shaikh, a giant of Marxian economics and professor at The New School in New York, passed away last week. His father served in the Foreign Service as a result of which his family moved around frequently, through Malaysia, Canada, Kuwait, and finally the US. It was in Kuwait, he would later say in a biographical note from 2016, that economics first claimed him: standing amid the gleaming infrastructure of an oil economy, he could not reconcile the scale of wealth with the poverty of those who produced it. The obvious question was why. He spent the next half-century building an answer to this and its related questions. I came to Shaikh’s work first through an undergraduate class: Aasim Sajjad Akhtar’s Political Economy of Development and Underdevelopment course, which featured Shaikh’s short four-page elaboration of Marx’s theory of exploitation published in a 1990 reader on Marxian economics compiled by Eatwell, Milgate, and Newman. It was only later on, after having joined academia myself, that I picked up a more sustained interest in his political economy contributions. Many of these were based on the workings of the advanced capitalist world, but to me it felt possible — via a universalist understanding of the capital-labour relation that characterises our shared modernity — that one could recover a broader insight and logic extendable to other contexts as well. His magnum opus, Capitalism: Competition, Conflict, Crises, published by Oxford in 2016 after nearly 20 years of writing, is not an easy book. It runs into nearly 1,000 pages and I have only been able to digest parts of it, a process aided greatly (and almost singularly) by his video lectures on YouTube. However, its central propositions are clear enough to state plainly — capitalism is driven by the pursuit of profit as a structural consideration. Firms invest, hire, fire, pollute, underpay, and cut corners not out of some moral imperative or ethical inadequacies, but because competition demands it. Competition, Shaikh insisted, is quite unlike the “decorous ballet” of textbook economics. It is a war, fought with prices, wages, lobbying, disinformation, and whatever else gives one firm an edge over another. In this universe, marked as it is by war, it’s a bit difficult to model markets as tending towards equilibrium (as orthodoxy usually claims). Shaikh, instead, argued that rather than any form of stasis, capitalism fluctuates, overshoots, crashes, recovers, and overshoots again. What is worth celebrating in Anwar Shaikh’s work is his insistence that economics is never neutral. Mainstream accounts tend to view these as ‘failures’ (of regulation or rationality). Someone like Shaikh, on the other hand, would see these as systemic features of a mode of production built on separating the producers of value from the means of production. His writings on so-called externalities generated by this systemic feature of competition are worth dwelling on, given the cost-of-living and ecological crises plaguing the planet. Orthodox economics treats pollution, low wages, and dangerous working conditions as costs that firms impose on society from outside the market, ie, as unfortunate side effects, correctable with the right regulations. Shaikh went as far as calling this view of externality a conceptual fraud. Rather than by accident, a firm pollutes because the alternative — investing in cleaner production — costs money that would otherwise be profit. The extraction and pollution are thus internal to how profit works. The same point has also been made at a more philosophical level by theorist Alysa Battistoni, who argues how nature is classified as a “free gift” under capitalism, ie, as something that does not carry with it the moral force of reciprocity or care (unlike a real gift). Beyond the intricate debates with the mainstream, what is worth celebrating in Shaikh’s work is his insistence that economics is never neutral. In his own words, he asserted that “there is no such thing as a value-free or socially neutral economics”. Every model encodes assumptions about how society works and who it works for. The amnesty schemes, the short-lived consumption-led booms, the stabilisation programmes that periodically arrive with the IMF, the growth targets announced at press conferences, the optimistic narratives about investor confidence and trickle-down are all consequences of choices made in a particular direction and for particular interests. Shaikh spent his career mapping those choices with a view to uncovering their systemic root in the unceasing motivation for profit. By implication, he ends up showing how reformist ‘tinkering’ that seeks to curtail externalities and fallouts is ultimately futile, and how a far more fundamental overhaul is required. Shaikh was educated partly at St Patrick’s in Karachi, before finishing his schooling in New York, his undergraduate at Princeton, his doctoral studies at Columbia, and a long career of teaching and research at the New School for Social Research in New York. During that time, he was always on the heterodox edge of the discipline, and concerned with abstract theory, which explains why his work never found the same recognition in a society that otherwise rushes to embrace high-achievers with even the most ephemeral of connections to Pakistan. However, that biography — from Karachi to a position of heterodox criticality in American academic life — carries a relevant resonance right now. In the face of geopolitical and economic reordering, the questions of whose economics we use, the viability of its long-held orthodoxies, and what they are actually deployed for, matter more urgently in Pakistan and the world at large than at any point in the recent past. It is then truly unfortunate that we have lost one of the clearest thinkers available on such questions. The writer teaches politics and sociology at Lums.
articles.author: Umair Javed

articles.title: Rebuilding values
articles.content: AT a time when good news is scarce, it was gratifying to see Navanethem ‘Navi’ Pillay receive the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. Pillay is a South African judge at the International Court of Justice and former UN high commissioner for human rights. She chaired the UN Commission of Inquiry that concluded last year that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. Such symbolic support for justice, human rights, and international law has been much wanting in recent years. Sadly, Pillay’s prize can also be perceived as a eulogy for international rule of law, which has been flagrantly disregarded, particularly in conflict contexts — from the targeting of civilian infrastructure to the use of chemical weapons and genocidal acts. As if to ring the death knell of the rules-based order, hours after Pillay received the honour, the US sanctioned the International Criminal Court (ICC), a punitive measure that would make it impossible for the court to function. That we now inhabit a multipolar, post-liberal democratic world order is evident. But moments like these highlight the extent to which the world we’ve known has been torn asunder. The collapse of liberal democratic norms leaves a vacuum which countries must now consider how to fill. This is not all bad — liberal democratic frameworks had imperial overtones, prioritised unfettered economic growth at the expense of social welfare and the planet, and engendered hypocrisy because those touting them were often unlikely to abide by them. But what has come in their wake is authoritarianism and a hyper-privileging of national sovereignty of the kind that enables the US — never a member state of the ICC — to declare the court a “rogue” institution. With World Values Day looming this Thursday, the question to ask is whether countries will use the world order vacuum to refresh national values in this era of national sovereignty. The speed of developments in these uncertain times means that nations rarely get time to reflect or publicly debate before taking decisions in a way that allows for alignment with national values or sovereign principles. With each destabilising development, whether invasions, pandemics or natural disasters, realpolitik reigns. National values that work for all must emerge organically. Today’s conflict and energy dynamics lead to expedient defence pacts, the pervasiveness of AI forces countries to sign up to global technology governance frameworks, and the stop-start flow of climate finance leads nations to make ambitious climate commitments. Little heed is paid to whether these policy decisions cohere and complement or contradict and undermine each other. In recent decades, the onus to cohere was less; the liberal democratic framework, with all its flaws and flows of money, offered some coherence — rule of law, rights, justice, but also individualism and rampant capitalist growth. But in its absence, the centre will not hold. This is why an intentional revisiting of national values may be welcome. The idea may cause shudders. National values in recent memory have been the bogeymen of authoritarians and dictators, imposed from the top down. Think of nations that have doubled down on alternative value systems, and places like Afghanistan and North Korea come to mind. National values that work for all must emerge organically from tradition, practice, a nuanced understanding of history and a desire to progressively engage with national documents such as constitutions. They must be inclusive, dynamic and open to challenge, and reflected across policy, law, and curricula. The best values are the products of difficult reckonings — truth and reconciliation proceedings, high-profile trials. This is a tall order for states like Pakistan that are ‘takers’ of political stances, standards, and policies. Ironically, it seems as if the thing that will replace the coherence of the liberal democratic world order will be AI’s rampaging monoculture. As all knowledge production, financial systems, and policymaking draw from the same well of AI slop, a consistency will emerge from the omnipresence of Big Tech and LLMs. Don’t ask me what that will look like. Instead, let’s look at an example of what values emerge when all state structures, humanitarian norms and justice are stripped away. The horrific and hugely underreported conflict in Sudan has led to the emergence of the country’s Emergency Response Rooms, strong Nobel Peace Prize contenders alongside Pillay. These are among the few sources of relief in Sudan, offering food, healthcare, schooling, counselling, and protection. These organisations are staffed by 26,000 volunteers and have grown from community kitchens and pandemic-era clinics into the primary solace from the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. Perhaps a return to the most basic values is the best way forward. The writer is a political and integrity risk analyst.
articles.author: Huma Yusuf

articles.title: Tax game
articles.content: FOR decades, the FBR has found itself stuck in a loop of introducing a series of simplified schemes to bring the vast informal sector into the tax net, only to watch them fall flat. The latest initiative, the Fixed Tax Asaan Scheme for traders, offered a simplified filing process, a flat one per cent tax on turnover, and immunity from routine audits. Yet, despite targeting an estimated 3.5 million eligible traders, only a few thousand enrolled, generating a negligible amount of tax against a target of Rs50 billion. To understand why well-intentioned schemes consistently fail, we must look beyond administrative sprints and examine the dynamics between taxpayers and the tax collector. In a strategic environment, players choose their actions based on expected payoffs. An analysis of the tax system under a game-theoretic framework, pioneered in Pakistan by renowned economist Dr Hafiz Pasha, helps explain how taxpayers develop strategies to counter the efforts of tax authorities. Consider, for example, the distinction between filers and non-filers, introduced to encourage greater formality. In essence, it is a weak policy lever: it penalises not being on the Active Taxpayers List rather than concealing income. An individual facing this distinction has three broad strategies: file honestly, file a return declaring nil or very little taxable income, or remain outside the tax system altogether. Honest filing can be the costliest option because it exposes income and assets to greater tax scrutiny. Staying outside the system, meanwhile, attracts higher tax rates on transactions such as property and vehicle purchases and certain financial transactions. The third option of filing with minimal declared income may be the cheapest route. Given the perception of FBR’s limited enforcement capacity, it may be a preferred strategy. Interestingly, the evidence also supports this. Income tax return filing has risen sharply, from around 2m returns in 2018 to about 6m now. Yet tax payments associated with return filing have not always kept pace with the growth in the number of filers. Traders are smarter than the FBR. This should be recognised. Similar is the case with the recent Tax Asaan Scheme for traders. The FBR attempted to break the informality trap through incentives. By reducing compliance costs and offering audit protection, alongside a green plate as a visible identifier for compliant businesses, the scheme sought to lower barriers to entry and make participation in the formal economy safer and mutually beneficial. However, despite these incentives, the FBR has failed to establish a cooperative equilibrium. Traders responded poorly to the scheme, which is an important lesson: making compliance cheaper and easier does not automatically make it attractive. A trader faces two choices. The first is to enter the tax system, declare turnover, pay tax, and establish a documented financial identity. The second is to remain outside the system. If staying outside carries little expected cost, the latter may still offer the greater payoff. Traders are smarter than the FBR. This should be recognised. The FBR plays within fixed parameters, while taxpayers have many more ways to adjust their strategies and work around them. Moreover, the FBR may be myopic, driven by the immediate pressure to meet revenue targets, while businesses consider a much longer time horizon. Perhaps the most serious issue with the design of this scheme is its time horizon. Traders have concerns about the next round of the game. They do not view tax compliance as a one-off decision; they evaluate it as a repeated game. Their primary concern may not be the paperwork required today, but the longer-term implications of documentation. They fear that disclosing the true scale of their businesses now could enable the government to change the rules in future rounds, requiring them to account for their sources of wealth, personal assets, and expenditure. They have legitimate concerns about policy continuity: will the 1pc tax rate remain unchanged? Will audit exemptions continue? Could the information disclosed today later be used for broader tax assessments? If the FBR wants a genuinely cooperative equilibrium, it must move beyond ad hoc, short-term schemes and focus on restructuring the underlying payoffs. It should prioritise meaningful tax reforms over the pursuit of immediate revenue targets, with greater emphasis on policy stability and predictability. Taxpayers must be given credible assurance that the rules will not later be changed in ways that penalise those who voluntarily enter the formal system.
articles.author: Farooq Arby

articles.title: Perilous misstep
articles.content: THE federal government on Sunday made good on its threat to dismiss an elected government and impose governor’s rule and emergency in KP. The presidentobliged. The head of state, the only civilian elected twice to that office, has now imposed governor’s rule three times: Punjab in 2009, Balochistan in 2013, and now KP — though the ruling PML-N is the main driver behind the latest move. His party, the PPP, has done so six times in the short history of Pakistani democracy, the others being in 1973 (Balochistan), 1975 (the then NWFP), and 1994 (again, KP). There is, therefore, nothing novel about Sunday’s move. However, it is a measure that has never achieved what its authors intended, and has more often than not backfired. That, perhaps, is why even those unsympathetic to the PTI government in Peshawar had been warning Islamabad not to take this step. In going ahead with it, the centre assumes responsibility for any blowback. The imposition of governor’s rule in Balochistan in 1973 is instructive. In February of that year, the then prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto dismissed the Balochistan government led by Sardar Attaullah Mengal, and also removed the then governor, Mir Ghaus Bakhsh Bizenjo. The centre ruled directly through Nawab Akbar Khan Bugti and sent in the army, fuelling an already smouldering insurgency. Many elected Baloch leaders turned separatist. The province never really recovered. KP is not Balochistan, and the PTI is no separatist movement. But the parallel of an elected leadership being swept aside on the pretext of security is unmistakable. The experience of the 1973 decision should be seen as a warning that this is how estrangement from the federation begins. There is no political justification for governor’s rule. If the authorities felt terrorism was increasing in some tribal districts and adjoining areas, they could have limited themselves to imposing a targeted emergency under Article 232, as they have already done. To deprive an entire province of its elected government is not only undemocratic; it can also be severely counterproductive, as history shows. The stated reason for Sunday’s decision is terrorism. The real target is perceived to be the only provincial government the opposition held, and the agitation it was leading. The PTI government may have faltered on several fronts, but in a democratic society, those failings are supposed to be addressed through the electoral process, not through executive fiat. Under Article 234, the proclamation lapses within two months unless parliament approves it. That is where this ill-considered action should be challenged on principle: lawmakers would do well to scrutinise it, and the courts to test whether the constitutional threshold was actually met. Islamabad must extricate itself from this quagmire before it deepens, and leave KP’s governance to those its people have elected to oversee it.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Import fraud
articles.content: THE under-invoicing of imports from China is not an allegation. It is an open secret in Pakistan’s markets — one that has been known for years. The gap between imports recorded from China and what China itself reports exporting is estimated to be in the range of $3.5-5bn in any single year. The Faisalabad loom owners have described this practice as one of the reasons their business is suffering. Yarn and cloth are the visible case, but the practice runs through the entire import trade from China — from machinery parts and chemicals to electronics, tyres, and household goods. Traders declare a fraction of the true value, pay duty and sales tax on that fraction, and sell at prices no domestic competitor can match. It could not happen at this scale without Customs. Valuation is checked at the port. When the same understatement recurs across the same products, importers, clearing agents, and officers who pass the consignments, year after year, it points past carelessness to facilitation. The damage is easy to trace. The exchequer loses duty and tax every day. Local manufacturers are forced to compete against goods whose prices have been shaved by a pen stroke. Mills close, looms are sold, workers go home. Then the same industry is told to become competitive and increase exports. It cannot, while its home market is being undercut by tax evasion that the state declines to acknowledge. It also corrupts what the country knows about itself. Imports are undercounted, so the trade deficit and the revenue gap are misstated, and policy is built on wrong numbers. The tools are already in place. Pakistan and China operate an electronic data exchange between their Customs administrations, and Islamabad has asked Beijing for real-time data. Applied to every shipment, not just textiles, comparing the Chinese export declaration with the Pakistani goods declaration would show mismatches in value and quantity at once. Large gaps should mean investigation, penalties, and prosecution. It is an argument for collecting what the law already requires, from everyone, equally. Cheaper power and easier credit mean little to a producer who is underpriced at the border. The government has assured the loom owners that their problems will be resolved. Controlling under-invoicing at the Pakistan-China border should be a good start.
articles.author: Editorial
